title: Diffusion Posterior Sampling with Uncertain Forward Models

paper.title: Diffusion Posterior Sampling with Uncertain Forward Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion posterior samplers reconstruct signals by combining a pretrained diffusion prior with a measurement likelihood specified by a forward model and a noise model.
Calibration and reference data can characterize uncertainty in the forward model’s parameters, such as blur kernels or detector responses.
Fixing these parameters at estimated values leaves their uncertainty out of the likelihood, and parameter errors are thus absorbed into the reconstruction.
We introduce an uncertainty-aware likelihood (UAL), a Gaussian approximation to the marginal likelihood obtained by integrating over the uncertain parameters.
For each candidate signal, UAL propagates parameter uncertainty into a structured measurement covariance, reducing the quadratic penalty along residual directions that parameter variation can explain.
Existing samplers can use UAL in their data updates while
retaining their pretrained diffusion priors and sampling schedules.
Under a fixed Gaussian nuisance model, we bound likelihood error from linearization and average divergence between the exact marginal and UAL posteriors.
We compare samplers with and without UAL across six inverse problems spanning Gaussian and motion deblurring, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and fluorescence microscopy, and find improvements in reconstruction and ensemble prediction.
UAL reduces geometric mean MSE by 9% to 20% across samplers in the main Gaussian-deblurring setting and by 51% to 92% in motion deblurring when non-blind samplers use the population-mean kernel.
In motion deblurring, DAPS and PnP-DM with UAL also give 6.2 to 6.4 dB higher ensemble-mean PSNR than published BlindDPS and Fast Diffusion EM.
On the ablation set, UAL outperforms trace-matched isotropic inflation for PnP-DM in both deblurring tasks; in motion deblurring, it also exceeds the best-tested fixed scalar data weighting by 3.3 dB for PnP-DM and 4.2 dB for DAPS in average PSNR.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion posterior samplers reconstruct signals by combining a pretrained diffusion prior ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) with a measurement likelihood specified by a forward model and an observation noise model ( Chung et al., 2023b ; Wu et al., 2024 ) . Parameters in the forward model, such as a blur kernel or detector response, can remain uncertain after calibration. We treat these quantities as nuisance parameters: they affect the measurements but estimating them is not an explicit goal. Calibration and reference data provide nuisance parameter estimates and can also describe their uncertainty. Fixing these quantities at one estimate, however, leaves that uncertainty out of the reconstruction likelihood. A reconstruction process can then distort the signal to fit components of residuals caused by nuisance parameter error. In motion deblurring, for example, a kernel bank describes variation in blur direction and extent across exposures. For a candidate image and a fixed kernel, the residual between the observed and predicted measurements combines image error, kernel error, and observation noise. A point likelihood, evaluated at one fixed kernel, penalizes this residual using only the observation noise model. For each candidate image, however, the kernel statistics and forward model predict correlated measurement changes caused by kernel variation. Residuals along these predicted directions provide weaker evidence of image error than residuals with the same observation-noise penalty that kernel variation cannot explain, so they should receive smaller quadratic penalties. The same effect arises in CT, where uncertainty in the flat and dark reference fields used for calibration changes the corrected projections even for fixed acquired data ( Shi et al., 2026 ) . Non-blind diffusion posterior samplers condition on a fixed measurement model ( Chung et al., 2023b ; Kawar et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , whereas blind methods sample or estimate the nuisance parameters together with the signal ( Chung et al., 2023a ; Murata et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Some blind samplers, such as BlindDPS, train an additional diffusion prior for the nuisance parameters ( Chung et al., 2023a ) . We instead marginalize forward-model parameters using an uncertainty model specified by calibration and reference information. Let x x denote the unknown signal, y y the measurements, ψ \psi the nuisance parameters, and q q a fixed uncertainty distribution for ψ \psi . The marginal likelihood is p marg ​ ( y ∣ x ) = 𝔼 ψ ∼ q ​ [ p ⁡ ( y ∣ x , ψ ) ] . p_{\mathrm{marg}}(y\mid x)=\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim q}\!\left[p(y\mid x,\psi)\right]. We introduce an uncertainty-aware likelihood (UAL), a Gaussian approximation to the nuisance-marginal likelihood that allows this direction-dependent weighting to be incorporated into existing diffusion posterior samplers. At a candidate signal, UAL linearizes the forward model in the nuisance parameters and uses their mean and covariance to construct the measurement likelihood. UAL is exact for affine nuisance dependence with Gaussian nuisance parameters and independent Gaussian observation noise; for non-Gaussian q q , UAL uses a Gaussian with the mean and covariance of the linearized measurement model (Section 3.1 ). For a fixed Gaussian nuisance model, we bound likelihood error from linearization and the resulting posterior divergence averaged over measurements from the model (Corollary 1 ). In a fixed-sensitivity linear model with known signal covariance and matched nuisance moments, the linear estimator using UAL minimizes mean squared reconstruction error among linear estimators, averaged over signals, nuisance parameters, and observation noise. At a fixed nuisance realization, the point-likelihood estimator can instead have lower error. For a single nuisance parameter and distinct estimators, we give the crossover distance from the nuisance mean in closed form (Appendix B ). UAL incorporates calibration and reference statistics into existing samplers’ data updates while retaining their pretrained priors and sampling schedules. We evaluate it with non-blind and blind diffusion samplers on synthetic and acquired measurements: Gaussian and motion deblurring, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and fluorescence microscopy. A simpler alternative inflates the observation-noise variance, which in effect weakens the data term. For PnP-DM, the best tested scalar inflation gives mean per-trajectory PSNR of 27.03 dB in Gaussian deblurring and 23.37 dB in motion deblurring. UAL adds variance only along directions that parameter variation can explain and gives 27.48 and 26.64 dB, respectively (Section 4.3 ). UAL also improves ensemble prediction: it lowers the mean CRPS, energy, and local variogram scores for every sampler and application in Table 1 . In Gaussian deblurring, UAL more closely matches the numerically marginalized likelihood and image score than the point and isotropic alternatives; covariance controls show the reconstruction benefit of structured, candidate-dependent weighting (Section 4.3 ). Applying UAL requires nuisance means and covariances and a forward model for propagating their variation; no additional diffusion-model training is needed. Covariance factorization reduces evaluation to forming and solving a system in nuisance coordinates. In the configurations of Table 22 , UAL takes at most three times the published sampler’s wall time per trajectory, except DAPS in motion deblurring at 7.1 times (Appendix D.8 ).

sections.heading: Diffusion priors for inverse problems.
sections.text: For fixed nuisance parameters ψ \psi and a signal prior p 0 ​ ( x ) p_{0}(x) that does not depend on ψ \psi , Bayes’ rule gives p ⁡ ( x ∣ y , ψ ) ∝ p ⁡ ( y ∣ x , ψ ) ​ p 0 ​ ( x ) p(x\mid y,\psi)\propto p(y\mid x,\psi)p_{0}(x) , where p ⁡ ( y ∣ x , ψ ) p(y\mid x,\psi) is the measurement likelihood. A pretrained diffusion model provides the prior through its denoisers or scores ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . The likelihood enters diffusion reconstruction through three common data-update forms: gradient guidance, data-fidelity optimization, and sampling-based updates. The likelihood at a noisy diffusion state x t x_{t} , p ⁡ ( y ∣ x t , ψ ) p(y\mid x_{t},\psi) , averages over possible clean signals and is generally intractable. DPS-style gradient guidance approximates it using a denoised estimate x ^ 0 ​ ( x t ) \hat{x}_{0}(x_{t}) and differentiates through that estimate ( Chung et al., 2023b ) . Π \Pi GDM propagates Gaussian approximations of clean-signal uncertainty through a fixed measurement operator to approximate the noisy-state likelihood ( Song et al., 2023 ) . Data-fidelity optimization solves a subproblem between denoising steps ( Zhu et al., 2023 ) . Sampling-based updates use the measurement in spectral coordinates ( Kawar et al., 2022 ) , in a split Gibbs sampler ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , or in annealed conditionals ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Diffusion priors with fixed-operator measurement models are also used in MRI ( Aali et al., 2025 ) , ultrasound ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , and CT ( Shi et al., 2026 ) . In these fixed-operator formulations, the likelihood conditions on a single nuisance-parameter value. For plug-and-play unadjusted Langevin sampling, Renaud et al. (2024) bound posterior error under mismatched measurement models and denoisers. UAL instead accounts for uncertainty in the forward-model parameters and enters each sampler through its existing data update (Section 3.2 ).

sections.heading: Blind inverse problems.
sections.text: Blind reconstruction treats the nuisance parameters as additional inference variables. Joint samplers place a prior on them and sample them with the signal: BlindDPS couples an image diffusion model and an operator diffusion model through a shared measurement likelihood ( Chung et al., 2023a ) ; GibbsDDRM alternates approximate posterior updates under a generic operator prior ( Murata et al., 2023 ) ; and PRISM pairs a measurement-conditioned kernel prior with an unconditional image prior in a split Gibbs sampler ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . Estimation methods fit them instead: Fast Diffusion EM updates the operator in a maximization step from image samples, with denoiser-based kernel regularization ( Laroche et al., 2024 ) ; and DMPlug optimizes the input to a pretrained diffusion generator jointly with the operator parameters ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . Kernel Diffusion samples a conditional kernel distribution and uses a non-blind method to reconstruct the image ( Sanghvi et al., 2025 ) . Under the same joint model, exact joint inference and exact marginalization give the same signal posterior; the methods differ in how nuisance uncertainty reaches the signal update. UAL approximates the marginal measurement likelihood from a specified uncertainty model, without training an additional diffusion model for the nuisance parameters. Appendix C gives the image and operator updates for the evaluated samplers.

sections.heading: Calibration and reference information.
sections.text: We use calibration data and reference samples to specify the means and covariances of uncertain forward-model parameters. Repeated CT flat and dark frames characterize variation in calibration fields ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , and principal-component representations of flat fields support dynamic projection normalization ( Nieuwenhove et al., 2015 ) . A motion-kernel bank describes variation in blur across exposures. ESPIRiT derives coil sensitivity maps from calibration data and permits multiple maps when a single-map model is insufficient ( Uecker et al., 2014 ) . Differences between the sound speeds provided with CUBDL acquisitions and their optimized values set the uncertainty scale for our PICMUS phantom reconstructions ( Hyun et al., 2021 ; Liebgott et al., 2016 ) . We represent the parameter variation by a distribution q q and use its mean and covariance to construct UAL (Section 3.1 ).

sections.heading: Marginalization and UAL.
sections.text: Errors-in-variables models account for measurement error in the model’s input variables ( Fuller, 1987 ) . Wiesel et al. (2008) derive maximum-likelihood estimators for linear regression with Gaussian uncertainty in the model matrix, and Beck and Eldar (2010) extend them to structured perturbations. Kumar et al. (2013) linearize sampling-location errors to obtain a Gaussian likelihood with signal-dependent variance, then update the variance weights in an iterative linear estimator. Using Bayesian approximation-error modeling ( Kaipio and Somersalo, 2007 ; Kaipio and Kolehmainen, 2013 ; Nissinen et al., 2007 ) , Mozumder et al. (2016) approximately marginalize uncertain optical coefficients with an enhanced Gaussian error model whose moments are estimated from prior samples and held fixed during reconstruction. For partially known random blurs, covariance weighting gives the classical LMMSE restoration filter ( Galatsanos et al., 2000 ) . UAL adapts this Gaussian treatment of forward-model uncertainty to diffusion posterior sampling through existing samplers’ data updates, and we test it against numerical marginalization and scalar variance inflation.

sections.heading: Use in diffusion samplers.
sections.text: Across applications, UAL treats forward-model uncertainty in the same way: it propagates parameter variation into a measurement covariance. We incorporate UAL through each sampler’s published data update ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) , retaining its diffusion prior and sampling schedule. Appendix Table 4 compares the point likelihood and UAL. Appendix C specifies the parameter models, reference values, and sampler updates.

sections.heading: Reconstruction-risk analysis.
sections.text: In the linear model of Appendix B , with nuisance sensitivity held fixed as the signal varies, the linear estimator based on UAL minimizes mean squared reconstruction error among linear estimators for any nuisance distribution whose mean and covariance match the assumed ones (Proposition 4 ). For a fixed parameter realization near the mean, the point estimator can have lower error; Appendix B characterizes the crossover and the conditions for positive average gain when these moments are inaccurate.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental protocol
sections.text: We evaluate UAL at two levels: reconstruction and ensemble prediction in paired sampler comparisons (Section 4.2 ), and, at shared candidate images, likelihood and image-score accuracy against numerical nuisance marginalization (Section 4.3 ). Additional controls examine covariance structure, recomputation and differentiation, uncertainty level, and retained rank. Published denotes the released sampler and UAL its uncertainty-aware version; each pair uses the same measurement data, diffusion checkpoint, sampling schedule, step sizes, and reconstruction seeds. Deblurring, CT, MRI, and microscopy use 50 cases, and ultrasound uses the acquired PICMUS contrast and resolution phantoms provided with DRUS; each case has 12 reconstruction seeds. The fixed deblurring ablation set contains 16 images, with 12 paired reconstruction seeds per image. Appendix C gives forward models, nuisance models, and sampler updates. We report PSNR and SSIM both as the mean over trajectories and for the ensemble-mean reconstruction. CRPS, energy, and local variogram scores (lower is better) use the fair finite-ensemble estimators of Appendix C.7 , which also gives the scoring coordinates and interval construction; ultrasound uses native contrast and resolution metrics.

sections.heading: 4.2 Reconstruction across samplers and applications
sections.text: We compare the Published and UAL versions of DAPS, PnP-DM, DiffPIR, and BlindDPS for Gaussian and motion deblurring on FFHQ images ( Karras et al., 2019 ) (Table 1 ). The Gaussian setting uses kernel widths with mean s ¯ = 3 \bar{s}=3 pixels and standard deviation τ = 0.5 \tau=0.5 pixels. In motion deblurring, each non-blind pair uses the population-mean kernel, giving the two likelihoods the same mean response at a common candidate image. Motion deblurring also includes Fast Diffusion EM ( Laroche et al., 2024 ) , a blind sampler that estimates a kernel for each image. Its UAL image update uses the population-mean kernel instead, with covariance accounting for image and kernel uncertainty and their interaction. We estimate the kernel covariance and retain its leading 256 eigenmodes ( P = 256 P=256 ), with this rank fixed before the covariance-rank sweep (Section 4.3 ). For mean per-trajectory PSNR, UAL gives 28.84 dB for DAPS and 26.54 dB for PnP-DM, compared with 30.65 and 27.65 dB when the published samplers use the true kernel (Table 8 ). For CT, the gain persists when both versions use the same mean flat and dark reference fields (Appendix D ). For MRI under the Gaussian coil-sensitivity model, UAL gives the exact marginal measurement likelihood. The MRI reconstruction gains are small but consistent: all seven reported metrics improve, with pointwise 95% paired-bootstrap intervals excluding zero. On the acquired PICMUS ultrasound contrast phantom, UAL increases CNR from 9.929 to 12.363 dB and gCNR from 0.9141 to 0.9743.

sections.heading: Likelihood approximation.
sections.text: For Gaussian deblurring, we evaluate the published PnP-DM point likelihood, UAL, and isotropic inflation at common final reconstructions produced by the published sampler. Numerical nuisance marginalization provides the reference. The isotropic control retains the UAL mean and scales the observation-noise covariance to v ⋆ ​ ( x ) ​ Σ e v_{\star}(x)\Sigma_{e} , where v ⋆ ​ ( x ) = tr ⁡ ( Σ e − 1 ​ S ​ ( x ) ) / m v_{\star}(x)=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{e}^{-1}S(x))/m is the average measurement variance under UAL after noise whitening. The isotropic and UAL covariances therefore have the same whitened trace. Among Gaussian likelihoods with the same mean and covariance v ​ Σ e v\Sigma_{e} , this trace match minimizes the KL divergence from UAL (Remark 1 ). At final reconstructions, UAL’s mean relative image-score error is below 1% at every tested uncertainty level, compared with 6% to 15% for the point likelihood. Its mean absolute negative-log-likelihood error is also the lowest of the three likelihoods (Figure 2 a,b). During sampling, UAL also has the lowest mean relative image-score error at each of the five saved states and each uncertainty level. At later states, its mean error is at most 2%, compared with approximately 6% to 19% for the point likelihood (Figure 2 c). Across these common candidates, UAL more closely approximates both the marginalized log likelihood and its image score than the two alternatives. sections.heading: Covariance structure.
sections.text: We next test whether covariance structure improves reconstruction and ensemble prediction beyond increasing total variance, using the three likelihoods in deblurring with PnP-DM. UAL and the isotropic control both include Gaussian normalization and differentiate their signal-dependent covariance. UAL’s structured covariance increases per-trajectory PSNR and reduces CRPS relative to trace-matched isotropic inflation in both tasks (Table 2 ). We also test fixed noise-variance multipliers and, for each task, report the one with the highest mean per-trajectory PSNR on the same ablation set used for comparison. The best tested values give 27.029 dB ( v = 3 v=3 ) in Gaussian and 23.369 dB ( v = 48 v=48 ) in motion deblurring, compared with 27.475 and 26.641 dB for UAL (Appendix D.4 ). For DAPS in motion deblurring, the best tested multiplier of its data-term variance ( v = 48 v=48 ) gives 24.413 dB mean per-trajectory PSNR, compared with 28.631 dB for UAL on the ablation set. At the final UAL reconstructions in Gaussian deblurring with PnP-DM, nuisance variation adds about 20% to the average whitened measurement variance, carried by the two width-sensitivity responses (Appendix D.5 ). Trace-matched isotropic inflation distributes the same added variance uniformly in noise-whitened coordinates. Table 2: Covariance structure at matched whitened trace on the ablation set. sections.heading: Covariance updates and derivatives.
sections.text: In Gaussian deblurring with PnP-DM, two further controls separate recomputing the covariance from differentiating it (Table 3 ). Fixing the covariance at the published sampler’s ensemble mean removes nearly all of the PSNR gain and raises CRPS above the published sampler’s. Recomputing it at each candidate keeps the gain whether or not its derivatives are propagated. By contrast, the motion-deblurring controls for Fast Diffusion EM keep the population-mean kernel fixed: differentiating the covariance raises mean per-trajectory PSNR from 23.80 to 28.49 dB, and including the log determinant gives 29.10 dB (Appendix D.4 ). sections.heading: Matched uncertainty.
sections.text: In Gaussian deblurring with PnP-DM, UAL’s reconstruction advantage grows as the generating and modeled width uncertainty increase together (Figure 4 ). At τ = 1.5 \tau=1.5 pixels, UAL exceeds Published by 1.75 dB and Isotropic by 0.47 dB in mean per-trajectory PSNR (Table 18 ). In a separate comparison of three combinations of mean width and width uncertainty, UAL gives higher mean per-trajectory PSNR and lower CRPS for all four samplers (Table 19 ).

sections.heading: Covariance rank.
sections.text: The rank sweep with PnP-DM shows that a compact covariance representation preserves reconstruction quality in motion deblurring (Figure 4 ). The 256-mode representation retains 96% of the kernel variance. On the ablation set, it gives 26.641 dB mean per-trajectory PSNR, compared with 26.251 dB for 2048 modes. The corresponding mean wall times are 89.5 and 2171.3 seconds per trajectory, respectively. Figure 3: Reconstruction error under matched Gaussian-width uncertainty with PnP-DM at mean width 3 pixels. sections.heading: Sensitivity to nuisance moments.
sections.text: With Gaussian-deblurring observations fixed, PnP-DM with UAL gives mean per-trajectory PSNR between 27.408 and 27.475 dB across the tested changes to either the parameter mean or covariance scale, up to approximately 20%. The published sampler with the correct mean width gives 26.944 dB, below every tested UAL setting (Figure 12 ). Underestimating the mean width increases CRPS more than any of the tested covariance rescalings. Motion deblurring is similarly insensitive to 20% changes in covariance scale (Table 17 ).

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion and limitations
sections.text: UAL uses forward-model uncertainty to weight measurement-residual directions according to how well parameter variation can explain them. It enters existing samplers through their data updates without additional diffusion-model training, and it improves reconstruction in CT, MRI, and fluorescence microscopy and contrast in ultrasound. In controlled Gaussian and motion deblurring comparisons with PnP-DM, retaining covariance structure improves reconstruction beyond trace-matched isotropic inflation. Accounting for forward-model uncertainty improves ensemble prediction: UAL lowers the mean CRPS, energy, and local variogram scores in all 12 comparisons in Table 1 . For PnP-DM in Gaussian deblurring, UAL has lower mean relative image-score error than the published and isotropic likelihoods at the final reconstructions and every evaluated sampling state, using numerical marginalization as the reference. UAL’s accuracy and reconstruction benefit depend on the nuisance model and, for nonlinear nuisance dependence, on the local forward-model approximation. UAL adds computation that grows with the covariance rank and depends on the sampler (Appendix D.8 ). In deblurring, UAL keeps its gain under tested mean or covariance-scale errors of up to about 20% (Figure 12 , Table 17 ); a different motion-kernel population was not tested.

sections.heading: Appendix B Fixed-sensitivity reconstruction analysis
sections.text: Under matched nuisance moments, the UAL linear estimator minimizes average squared error among linear estimators; at a fixed nuisance realization its error can exceed the point estimator’s. We quantify this tradeoff and the reconstruction cost of covariance truncation.

sections.heading: Forward conventions.
sections.text: In Gaussian deblurring, DAPS, PnP-DM, and BlindDPS use zero-padded cross-correlation, with padding of 31 pixels before and 32 after each image dimension. DiffPIR’s released closed-form Fourier deblurring step requires circular convolution, so we retain that convention and generate its observations with it. Both members of each sampler pair receive the same observation. Motion observations use circular convolution. DAPS, PnP-DM, and DiffPIR use circular mean and mode operators. The DiffPIR likelihood step uses x + = ( x − + 1 ) / 2 x_{+}=(x_{-}+1)/2 and y + = ( y − + 1 ) / 2 y_{+}=(y_{-}+1)/2 , converting the stored [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] coordinates to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . For unit-sum circular convolution, A ​ 𝟏 = 𝟏 A\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1} , so y + = A ​ x + + e − / 2 y_{+}=Ax_{+}+e_{-}/2 . Consequently σ + = 0.01 \sigma_{+}=0.01 and Σ e , + = Σ e , − / 4 {\Sigma_{e,+}}={\Sigma_{e,-}}/4 . Its data-step output is converted back by x − = 2 ​ x + − 1 x_{-}=2x_{+}-1 before the diffusion update.

sections.heading: C.2 UAL in deblurring samplers
sections.text: Each sampler incorporates UAL’s measurement mean and covariance through its existing data update while retaining its pretrained diffusion prior and sampling schedule. Two PnP-DM controls in Gaussian deblurring separate covariance recomputation from differentiation. One recomputes covariance at each candidate while stopping its derivatives; the other fixes covariance at the ensemble mean of the published sampler’s 12 reconstructions. The latter reference is shared across that image’s reconstruction seeds; all controls use the same observations and evaluation images. A third control multiplies the point likelihood’s noise variance by v ∈ { 1 , 1.5 , 2 , 3 , 5 } v\in\{1,1.5,2,3,5\} on the ablation set. In motion deblurring, the noise-variance multipliers are v ∈ { 1 , 3 , 6 , 12 , 24 , 48 , 96 , 192 , 384 } v\in\{1,3,6,12,24,48,96,192,384\} on the ablation set. We compare the multipliers by mean per-trajectory PSNR, keeping the Langevin step size unchanged. Appendix D.4 reports the scalar-control results.

sections.heading: Data and calibration.
sections.text: We use the DM4CT synchrotron rock data ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , distributed through Zenodo. 3 3 3 https://zenodo.org/records/15420527 It contains 1200 1200 projections, 20 20 flat frames, and 20 20 dark frames. Our application uses 60 views and the released DM4CT synchrotron diffusion prior with DAPS ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . We follow the published DM4CT preprocessing and reference reconstructions. Published uses one flat and one dark frame; UAL uses the mean reference fields. Appendix D also compares both versions using those mean fields. Each CT case is a two-dimensional reconstruction from the same detector row across the 60 projection views. Here ψ \psi collects the flat and dark reference fields. For raw projection p p , flat field f f , and dark field d dark d_{\rm dark} , the calibration map acts elementwise as z ⁡ ( p , f , d dark ) = − a CT ​ log ⁡ max ⁡ { p − d dark f − d dark , t min } . z(p;f,d_{\rm dark})=-a_{\rm CT}\log\max\!\left\{\frac{p-d_{\rm dark}}{f-d_{\rm dark}},t_{\min}\right\}. (58) Here a CT a_{\rm CT} is the log-sinogram scale and t min t_{\min} is the transmission floor. The nuisance vector is ψ = ( f 𝖳 , d dark 𝖳 ) 𝖳 \psi=(f^{\mathsf{T}},d_{\rm dark}^{\mathsf{T}})^{\mathsf{T}} . From each set of N = 20 N=20 reference frames, we compute f ¯ = 1 N ​ ∑ j = 1 N f j , d ¯ dark = 1 N ​ ∑ j = 1 N d dark , j , \bar{f}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}f_{j},\qquad\bar{d}_{\rm dark}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}d_{{\rm dark},j}, F f \displaystyle F_{f} = [ f 1 − f ¯ , … , f N − f ¯ ] N − 1 , \displaystyle=\frac{[f_{1}-\bar{f},\ldots,f_{N}-\bar{f}]}{\sqrt{N-1}}, F d \displaystyle F_{d} = [ d dark , 1 − d ¯ dark , … , d dark , N − d ¯ dark ] N − 1 . \displaystyle=\frac{[d_{{\rm dark},1}-\bar{d}_{\rm dark},\ldots,d_{{\rm dark},N}-\bar{d}_{\rm dark}]}{\sqrt{N-1}}. The Gaussian reference-field model has μ = [ f ¯ d ¯ dark ] , Σ ψ = [ F f ​ F f 𝖳 0 0 F d ​ F d 𝖳 ] . \mu=\begin{bmatrix}\bar{f}\\ \bar{d}_{\rm dark}\end{bmatrix},\qquad\Sigma_{\psi}=\begin{bmatrix}F_{f}F_{f}^{\mathsf{T}}&0\\ 0&F_{d}F_{d}^{\mathsf{T}}\end{bmatrix}. These statistics are estimated once and shared across the reconstructions. We use frame-to-frame variability to model the uncertain flat and dark fields, with independent Gaussian fluctuations.

sections.heading: C.4 MRI with coil-map uncertainty
sections.text: We estimate coil-map variation by perturbing the calibration measurements and recalibrating the sensitivity maps. The resulting covariance determines the Gaussian coefficient model used in the Ambient DPS likelihood.

sections.heading: Data and forward model.
sections.text: We use multi-coil brain measurements from the NYU fastMRI Initiative ( Knoll et al., 2020 ; Zbontar et al., 2019 ) . We take the middle slice of each volume, apply coil-noise prewhitening and intensity normalization, and use the resulting k-space measurements, sampling mask, and sensitivity maps. Both versions use the released Ambient Diffusion checkpoint trained at acceleration 6, the released acceleration-8 masks, and the same coil-map calibration width and noise convention. Reference images are reconstructed from full k-space data using the released preparation procedure. We evaluate 50 T2-weighted brain volumes selected at random without replacement from the fastMRI validation set, excluding six development volumes. Here x x denotes the complex image. Here ℱ \mathcal{F} is the released orthonormal Fourier transform and M M is the sampling mask ( Aali et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: C.5 Ultrasound with sound-speed uncertainty
sections.text: Differences between submitted and optimized sound speeds in the CUBDL acquisitions set the uncertainty scale. We propagate nonlinear sound-speed variation at a fixed pilot reconstruction to obtain the per-mode variances used by DRUS.

sections.heading: Data and forward model.
sections.text: We use the acquired PICMUS contrast and resolution phantoms provided with the DRUS release and its linked supplement, with 12 paired trajectories per phantom ( Liebgott et al., 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Channel measurements y raw y_{\rm raw} and beamformed measurements y d y_{d} are related by y raw = H ⁡ ( c s ) ​ x + n , y d = B 0 ​ y raw = B 0 ​ H ​ ( c s ) ​ x + B 0 ​ n , B 0 = B ⁡ ( c s , 0 ) . y_{\mathrm{raw}}=H({c_{s}})x+n,\qquad y_{d}=B_{0}y_{\mathrm{raw}}=B_{0}H({c_{s}})x+B_{0}n,\qquad B_{0}=B({c_{s,0}}). The signal is reflectivity, the nuisance is ψ = c s \psi={c_{s}} , and 𝒜 ⁡ ( x , c s ) = B 0 ​ H ​ ( c s ) ​ x \mathcal{A}(x,{c_{s}})=B_{0}H({c_{s}})x . The reference sound speed is c s , 0 = 1540 ​ m / s {c_{s,0}}=1540\,\mathrm{m/s} . When varying c s {c_{s}} , we keep the beamformer B 0 B_{0} , channel-data layout, and measurement window fixed at their reference definitions. Only H ⁡ ( c s ) H({c_{s}}) changes. The reference beamformed operator is H d = B 0 ​ H ​ ( c s , 0 ) H_{d}=B_{0}H({c_{s,0}}) , with singular value decomposition H d = U d ​ S d ​ V d 𝖳 H_{d}=U_{d}S_{d}V_{d}^{\mathsf{T}} . The published DRUS spectral step uses a scalar noise model; the UAL replacement uses per-mode variances. The sound-speed uncertainty scale comes from the nine CUBDL 040GSE reference acquisitions ( Hyun et al., 2021 ) , MYO001--MYO006 and UFL003--UFL005 in the released workbook. 5 5 5 https://gitlab.com/dongwoon.hyun/cubdl/-/blob/master/datasets/CUBDL_Phantom_Details.xlsx For their submitted-minus-optimized speed offsets δ j = 1540 − c s , j opt \delta_{j}=1540-c_{s,j}^{\rm opt} , we compute δ ¯ = 1 9 ​ ∑ j = 1 9 δ j , σ c 2 = 1 8 ​ ∑ j = 1 9 ( δ j − δ ¯ ) 2 . \bar{\delta}=\frac{1}{9}\sum_{j=1}^{9}\delta_{j},\qquad\sigma_{c}^{2}=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{j=1}^{9}(\delta_{j}-\bar{\delta})^{2}. sections.heading: C.6 Fluorescence microscopy with pupil-phase uncertainty
sections.text: We reconstruct a thin two-dimensional fluorescent object from a blurred measurement. Five uncertain pupil-phase coefficients determine the point-spread function. Their prescribed Gaussian distribution defines the synthetic aberrations and the uncertainty propagated by UAL.

sections.heading: Reference images and measurements.
sections.text: We use four stacks from the CARE Planaria test data ( Weigert et al., 2018 ) . From the 192 available axial sections, we select 13, 13, 12, and 12 uniformly spaced sections from the four stacks in filename order. We take a central 256 × 256 256\times 256 crop from each section. Selection uses no reconstruction scores. The crop is mapped to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] using the minimum and maximum of its full source section, then used as the reference signal x x in y = A k ⁡ ( ψ ⋆ ) ​ x + e , e ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ e 2 ​ I ) , σ e = 0.02 , y=A_{k(\psi^{\star})}x+e,\qquad e\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{e}^{2}I),\qquad\sigma_{e}=0.02, (67) where A k A_{k} denotes circular convolution with kernel k k , and ψ ⋆ \psi^{\star} contains the realized pupil-phase coefficients. The reference is an acquired CARE image section; the aberrated measurement is generated by this forward model.

sections.heading: Optical model.
sections.text: The scalar pupil model uses wavelength λ em = 0.6 ​ μ ​ m \lambda_{\rm em}=0.6\,\mu{\rm m} , numerical aperture NA = 1.2 \mathrm{NA}=1.2 , refractive index n med = 1.33 n_{\rm med}=1.33 , and a fixed focal offset z f = 1 ​ μ ​ m z_{f}=1\,\mu{\rm m} . For normalized pupil coordinates ξ = ( u , v ) \xi=(u,v) in the unit disk, the phase is ϕ ⁡ ( ξ , ψ ) = ∑ j = 1 5 ψ j ​ Z ι j ​ ( ξ ) − 2 ​ π ​ z f ​ [ ( n med λ em ) 2 − ( NA λ em ) 2 ​ ‖ ξ ‖ 2 − n med λ em ] . \phi(\xi;\psi)=\sum_{j=1}^{5}\psi_{j}Z_{\iota_{j}}(\xi)-2\pi z_{f}\left[\sqrt{\left(\frac{n_{\rm med}}{\lambda_{\rm em}}\right)^{2}-\left(\frac{{\rm NA}}{\lambda_{\rm em}}\right)^{2}\|\xi\|^{2}}-\frac{n_{\rm med}}{\lambda_{\rm em}}\right]. (68) Here ι = ( 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 11 ) \iota=(5,6,7,8,11) selects unit-RMS Zernike modes in Noll ordering ( Noll, 1976 ) , and ψ j \psi_{j} is measured in phase radians. Writing r 2 = u 2 + v 2 r^{2}=u^{2}+v^{2} , the implemented modes are 6 ​ ( 2 ​ u ​ v ) \sqrt{6}(2uv) , 6 ​ ( u 2 − v 2 ) \sqrt{6}(u^{2}-v^{2}) , 8 ​ v ​ ( 3 ​ r 2 − 2 ) \sqrt{8}\,v(3r^{2}-2) , 8 ​ u ​ ( 3 ​ r 2 − 2 ) \sqrt{8}\,u(3r^{2}-2) , and 5 ​ ( 6 ​ r 4 − 6 ​ r 2 + 1 ) \sqrt{5}(6r^{4}-6r^{2}+1) . The focal offset is fixed; it is not one of the nuisance coordinates. Let Ω \Omega be the points of a 64 × 64 64\times 64 midpoint grid inside the unit disk. A positive-exponent matrix Fourier transform gives the field at detector positions 𝐫 \mathbf{r} : h ψ ​ ( 𝐫 ) = ∑ ξ ∈ Ω exp ⁡ ( i ​ ϕ ​ ( ξ , ψ ) ) ​ exp ⁡ ( 2 ​ π ​ i ​ NA λ em ​ 𝐫 𝖳 ​ ξ ) , k ⁡ ( ψ ) ​ [ 𝐫 ] = | h ψ ​ ( 𝐫 ) | 2 ∑ 𝐫 ′ | h ψ ​ ( 𝐫 ′ ) | 2 . h_{\psi}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{\xi\in\Omega}\exp\!\bigl(i\phi(\xi;\psi)\bigr)\exp\!\left(2\pi i\,\frac{{\rm NA}}{\lambda_{\rm em}}\mathbf{r}^{\mathsf{T}}\xi\right),\qquad k(\psi)[\mathbf{r}]=\frac{|h_{\psi}(\mathbf{r})|^{2}}{\sum_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}|h_{\psi}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})|^{2}}. (69) The detector grid has 65 × 65 65\times 65 samples with 0.1 ​ μ ​ m 0.1\,\mu{\rm m} spacing. The discrete kernel is normalized on this grid before circular convolution.

sections.heading: Aberration distribution and UAL.
sections.text: The five pupil-phase coefficients follow the prescribed Gaussian distribution q = 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ , Σ ψ ) , μ = ( 0.10 , − 0.10 , 0.05 , 0 , 0.10 ) 𝖳 , Σ ψ = 0.15 2 ​ I 5 . q=\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma_{\psi}),\qquad\mu=(0.10,-0.10,0.05,0,0.10)^{\mathsf{T}},\qquad\Sigma_{\psi}=0.15^{2}I_{5}. (70) This distribution generates the synthetic aberrations and provides the mean and covariance used by UAL. We linearize at ψ 0 = μ \psi_{0}=\mu , so the first-order mean correction vanishes. Independent observation noise is added to each measurement. One draw ψ ⋆ ∼ q \psi^{\star}\sim q and one noisy measurement are fixed per section and shared by both sampler versions and all 12 trajectories. To propagate phase uncertainty, we differentiate the optical intensity and its normalization. Define I ψ ​ ( 𝐫 ) = | h ψ ​ ( 𝐫 ) | 2 I_{\psi}(\mathbf{r})=|h_{\psi}(\mathbf{r})|^{2} and T ψ = ∑ 𝐫 I ψ ​ ( 𝐫 ) T_{\psi}=\sum_{\mathbf{r}}I_{\psi}(\mathbf{r}) . The pupil-field derivative at μ \mu is h j ​ ( 𝐫 ) = ∂ ψ j h ψ ​ ( 𝐫 ) | μ = i ​ ∑ ξ ∈ Ω Z ι j ​ ( ξ ) ​ e i ​ ϕ ​ ( ξ , μ ) ​ e 2 ​ π ​ i ​ ( NA / λ em ) ​ 𝐫 𝖳 ​ ξ . h_{j}(\mathbf{r})=\left.\partial_{\psi_{j}}h_{\psi}(\mathbf{r})\right|_{\mu}=\mathrm{i}\sum_{\xi\in\Omega}Z_{\iota_{j}}(\xi)e^{\mathrm{i}\phi(\xi;\mu)}e^{2\pi\mathrm{i}({\rm NA}/\lambda_{\rm em})\mathbf{r}^{\mathsf{T}}\xi}. The intensity and normalized-kernel derivatives are I j ​ ( 𝐫 ) \displaystyle I_{j}(\mathbf{r}) = 2 ​ Re ⁡ [ h μ ​ ( 𝐫 ) ¯ ​ h j ​ ( 𝐫 ) ] , \displaystyle=2\operatorname{Re}\!\left[\overline{h_{\mu}(\mathbf{r})}h_{j}(\mathbf{r})\right], κ j ​ ( 𝐫 ) \displaystyle\kappa_{j}(\mathbf{r}) = I j ​ ( 𝐫 ) − k ⁡ ( μ ) ​ [ 𝐫 ] ​ ∑ 𝐫 ′ I j ​ ( 𝐫 ′ ) T μ , b j = 0.15 κ j . \displaystyle=\frac{I_{j}(\mathbf{r})-k(\mu)[\mathbf{r}]\sum_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}I_{j}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})}{T_{\mu}},\qquad b_{j}=0.15\kappa_{j}. Each κ j \kappa_{j} sums to zero, so it changes the PSF shape while preserving unit sum. For a ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I 5 ) a\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{5}) , linearization gives k ⁡ ( μ + 0.15 ​ a ) ≈ k ⁡ ( μ ) + ∑ j a j ​ b j k(\mu+0.15a)\approx k(\mu)+\sum_{j}a_{j}b_{j} . Under this linearization, the conditional measurement model is y | x , a ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( A k ⁡ ( μ ) ​ x + ∑ j = 1 5 a j ​ A b j ​ x , σ e 2 ​ I ) . y\mid x,a\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(A_{k(\mu)}x+\sum_{j=1}^{5}a_{j}A_{b_{j}}x,\sigma_{e}^{2}I\right). Integrating over a a gives y ¯ ​ ( x ) = A k ⁡ ( μ ) ​ x , U ⁡ ( x ) = [ A b 1 ​ x , … , A b 5 ​ x ] , S ⁡ ( x ) = σ e 2 ​ I + U ⁡ ( x ) ​ U ​ ( x ) 𝖳 . \bar{y}(x)=A_{k(\mu)}x,\qquad U(x)=[A_{b_{1}}x,\ldots,A_{b_{5}}x],\qquad S(x)=\sigma_{e}^{2}I+U(x)U(x)^{\mathsf{T}}. (71) We prepare the reference kernel and its five scaled derivative kernels b j b_{j} once. The reduced system is 5 × 5 5\times 5 and is evaluated by Cholesky factorization in double precision.

sections.heading: Released sampler and UAL update.
sections.text: Both versions use PnP-DM ( Wu et al., 2024 ) with the ED-Diff CARE checkpoint ( Luo et al., 2026 ) and the same mean kernel k ⁡ ( μ ) k(\mu) . For candidate image u u , with d ⁡ ( u ) = y − A k ⁡ ( μ ) ​ u d(u)=y-A_{k(\mu)}u , the UAL likelihood step uses ℓ UAL ​ ( u , y ) = 1 2 ​ d ​ ( u ) 𝖳 ​ S ​ ( u ) − 1 ​ d ​ ( u ) + 1 2 ​ log ​ det S ⁡ ( u ) + m 2 ​ log ⁡ ( 2 ​ π ) , \ell_{\rm UAL}(u;y)=\tfrac{1}{2}d(u)^{\mathsf{T}}S(u)^{-1}d(u)+\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det S(u)+\tfrac{m}{2}\log(2\pi), with S ⁡ ( u ) S(u) from ( 71 ). At outer iterate x ( k ) x^{(k)} , the conditional target is proportional to exp ⁡ [ − ℓ UAL ​ ( u , y ) − ‖ u − x ( k ) ‖ 2 / ( 2 ​ ρ k 2 ) ] \exp[-\ell_{\rm UAL}(u;y)-\|u-x^{(k)}\|^{2}/(2\rho_{k}^{2})] . Its Langevin gradient includes the covariance derivatives, as in Algorithm 4 . The UAL likelihood step takes 100 steps of size 10 − 4 10^{-4} per likelihood update. Algorithm 3 gives the shared outer sampler; the diffusion-prior update is unchanged from the released method. Both versions use 100 outer iterations in total, including 40 burn-in iterations, and the variance-preserving SDE mode with 100 prior steps. The coupling scale ρ k \rho_{k} starts at 10, decays by a factor of 0.9 0.9 per iteration, and has minimum 0.3 0.3 . For each seed, we retain the last sample returned by PnP-DM. Twelve paired seeds, 0 through 11, give 600 reconstructions per version. The realized aberration coefficients and true PSFs are used only in measurement generation and evaluation.

sections.heading: Diffusion prior, scoring, and data access.
sections.text: The released ED-Diff model has one input channel, 64 base channels, three residual blocks per resolution level, and a 1,000-step linear diffusion schedule. For each prior update, we map the requested noise level to the nearest level on this schedule and convert the pretrained noise prediction to a clean-signal estimate, clipped to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] . No retraining is performed. PSNR and SSIM use data range 2 and are computed per trajectory before averaging within sections and across the 50 sections. The reference sections come from CARE’s original test stacks. The released ED-Diff prior is pretrained on high-SNR images ( Luo et al., 2026 ) . CARE data are distributed through the Edmond repository, doi:10.17617/3.FDFZOF , whose metadata specify CC0 1.0. The ED-Diff code and checkpoint are obtained through the authors’ release . The examined release does not specify a separate redistribution license for the checkpoint.

sections.heading: C.7 Evaluation metrics and reporting
sections.text: Reported 95% intervals use 20,000 paired bootstrap resamples of images for deblurring, detector rows within the same acquisition for CT, and scans for MRI, after computing each case’s reconstruction and ensemble scores. Ablation error bars are standard errors across the ablation set. The microscopy whiskers in Figure 1 resample the 50 sections in pairs and describe variation within these sections. Per-stack gains provide a separate descriptive comparison. Ultrasound whiskers in Figure 1 show one standard error of the paired differences across the 12 contrast-phantom trajectories. Following the DRUS evaluation protocol, we report contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), generalized contrast-to-noise ratio (gCNR), and speckle SNR on the contrast phantom, and axial and lateral full width at half maximum (FWHM) on the resolution phantom. For one case, let x ^ ( 1 ) , … , x ^ ( R ) ∈ ℝ n \widehat{x}^{(1)},\ldots,\widehat{x}^{(R)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} be the vectorized reconstructions in scoring coordinates with R ≥ 2 R\geq 2 , and let x ⋆ x^{\star} be the reference. We distinguish the average trajectory score from the score of the ensemble-mean reconstruction: metric ¯ = 1 R ​ ∑ r = 1 R metric ⁡ ( x ^ ( r ) , x ⋆ ) , metric ens = metric ⁡ ( x ^ ens , x ⋆ ) . \overline{\operatorname{metric}}=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\operatorname{metric}(\widehat{x}^{(r)},x^{\star}),\qquad\operatorname{metric}_{\mathrm{ens}}=\operatorname{metric}(\widehat{x}_{\mathrm{ens}},x^{\star}). (72) This distinction applies to both PSNR and SSIM. For the real-valued tasks, x ^ ens = R − 1 ​ ∑ r x ^ ( r ) \widehat{x}_{\mathrm{ens}}=R^{-1}\sum_{r}\widehat{x}^{(r)} . For MRI, individual magnitude reconstructions are used for per-trajectory PSNR and SSIM and for the three fair ensemble scores. For ensemble-mean PSNR and SSIM, we first average the complex reconstructions and then take the magnitude. Case-level scores are averaged over the reported cases. For a reconstruction z z , we use MSE ⁡ ( z , x ⋆ ) = 1 n ​ ‖ z − x ⋆ ‖ 2 2 , PSNR ⁡ ( z , x ⋆ ) = 10 ​ log 10 ​ D 2 MSE ⁡ ( z , x ⋆ ) , \operatorname{MSE}(z,x^{\star})=\frac{1}{n}\|z-x^{\star}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\operatorname{PSNR}(z,x^{\star})=10\log_{10}\frac{D^{2}}{\operatorname{MSE}(z,x^{\star})}, (73) where D D is the task-specific PSNR peak. If Δ ¯ PSNR \overline{\Delta}_{\mathrm{PSNR}} is the mean paired PSNR gain, the geometric mean of the UAL-to-original MSE ratios is 10 − Δ ¯ PSNR / 10 10^{-\overline{\Delta}_{\mathrm{PSNR}}/10} . We use this relation for the relative MSE reductions in the Abstract and Introduction. For deblurring and microscopy, PSNR and SSIM use the data range 2 for intensities in [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] . CT uses the reference-image range for both; MRI uses the reference-image maximum for PSNR and its range for SSIM. SSIM uses the scikit-image default window settings; color-image scores are averaged over channels. The fair finite-ensemble estimators of the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) and the energy score ( Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ; Ferro, 2014 ) use off-diagonal ensemble pairs: CRPS f \displaystyle\operatorname{CRPS}_{\mathrm{f}} = 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n [ 1 R ​ ∑ r = 1 R | x ^ i ( r ) − x i ⋆ | − 1 R ⁡ ( R − 1 ) ​ ∑ r < s | x ^ i ( r ) − x ^ i ( s ) | ] , \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}|\widehat{x}_{i}^{(r)}-x_{i}^{\star}|-\frac{1}{R(R-1)}\sum_{r<s}|\widehat{x}_{i}^{(r)}-\widehat{x}_{i}^{(s)}|\right], (74) ES f \displaystyle\operatorname{ES}_{\mathrm{f}} = 1 R ​ ∑ r = 1 R ‖ x ^ ( r ) − x ⋆ ‖ 2 − 1 R ⁡ ( R − 1 ) ​ ∑ r < s ‖ x ^ ( r ) − x ^ ( s ) ‖ 2 . \displaystyle=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\|\widehat{x}^{(r)}-x^{\star}\|_{2}-\frac{1}{R(R-1)}\sum_{r<s}\|\widehat{x}^{(r)}-\widehat{x}^{(s)}\|_{2}. (75) The energy score uses the Euclidean norm of the full image vector, without an additional dimension normalization. For the local variogram score, define the pair features v i ​ j ( r ) = | x ^ i ( r ) − x ^ j ( r ) | 1 / 2 v_{ij}^{(r)}=|\widehat{x}_{i}^{(r)}-\widehat{x}_{j}^{(r)}|^{1/2} and v i ​ j ⋆ = | x i ⋆ − x j ⋆ | 1 / 2 v_{ij}^{\star}=|x_{i}^{\star}-x_{j}^{\star}|^{1/2} using the variogram construction of Scheuerer and Hamill (2015) . Let v ¯ i ​ j = R − 1 ​ ∑ r v i ​ j ( r ) \bar{v}_{ij}=R^{-1}\sum_{r}v_{ij}^{(r)} . For each offset g g , let 𝒫 g \mathcal{P}_{g} contain the valid within-channel pixel pairs at that offset. We use lags 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 in the horizontal, vertical, and two diagonal directions, giving 20 offset groups. We use the fair estimator LVS f = 1 20 ​ ∑ g 1 | 𝒫 g | ​ ∑ ( i , j ) ∈ 𝒫 g [ ( v ¯ i ​ j − v i ​ j ⋆ ) 2 − 1 R ⁡ ( R − 1 ) ​ ∑ r = 1 R ( v i ​ j ( r ) − v ¯ i ​ j ) 2 ] . \operatorname{LVS}_{\mathrm{f}}=\frac{1}{20}\sum_{g}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{g}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_{g}}\left[(\bar{v}_{ij}-v_{ij}^{\star})^{2}-\frac{1}{R(R-1)}\sum_{r=1}^{R}(v_{ij}^{(r)}-\bar{v}_{ij})^{2}\right]. (76) Thus valid pairs and channels are averaged within each offset group, and the groups receive equal weight. Lower values of all three ensemble scores are better. sections.heading: D.1 Numerical likelihood reference
sections.text: For Figure 2 , we integrate the nonlinear Gaussian-blur likelihood over two independent positive-truncated-normal width distributions, with mean width 3 pixels and standard deviations τ ∈ { 0.25 , 0.5 , 1 , 1.5 } \tau\in\{0.25,0.5,1,1.5\} pixels. At fixed candidate x x and measurement y y , we center adaptive tensor-product Gauss–Hermite quadrature at a mode of p ⁡ ( ψ ∣ x , y ) ∝ q ⁡ ( ψ ) ​ p ​ ( y ∣ x , ψ ) p(\psi\mid x,y)\propto q(\psi)p(y\mid x,\psi) . We find the mode by L-BFGS-B with positive width bounds, starting from ( 3 , 3 ) (3,3) and ( 3 + τ , 3 − τ ) (3+\tau,3-\tau) pixels and retaining the solution with the lower negative log posterior. The Gaussian quadrature proposal h h has covariance given by the inverse of the symmetrized Hessian of − log ⁡ [ q ⁡ ( ψ ) ​ p ​ ( y ∣ x , ψ ) ] -\log[q(\psi)p(y\mid x,\psi)] , computed by centered finite differences of the nuisance gradient at the mode. The transformed quadrature weights include q ⁡ ( ψ ) / h ⁡ ( ψ ) q(\psi)/h(\psi) , with zero weight outside the positive-width support. The likelihood calculations use the same kernel grid, boundary convention, crop, and noise standard deviation 0.02 0.02 as the paired reconstructions. Writing g = ∇ x ​ log ​ p ​ ( y ∣ x ) g=\nabla_{x}\log p(y\mid x) and ℓ = − log ⁡ p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) \ell=-\log p(y\mid x) , the plotted errors are 100 ​ ‖ g − g ref ‖ 2 / ‖ g ref ‖ 2 100\|g-g_{\rm ref}\|_{2}/\|g_{\rm ref}\|_{2} percent and | ℓ − ℓ ref | / m |\ell-\ell_{\rm ref}|/m nats per measurement, with m = 3 × 256 × 256 m=3\times 256\times 256 . The reference score is the nuisance-posterior-weighted average of the conditional image scores. At each uncertainty level, all three likelihoods use the same candidate and observation. We average errors over trajectories within each image before computing the mean and SE across images. We checked numerical convergence for all 768 final candidate–observation pairs in Figure 2 a,b by increasing the quadrature order from 5 to 9 per width coordinate. The largest observed changes were 5.82 × 10 − 11 5.82\times 10^{-11} nats in energy and 5.77 × 10 − 12 5.77\times 10^{-12} in the relative ℓ 2 \ell_{2} score change. These changes with quadrature order are far below the plotted approximation errors. To compare likelihood accuracy during sampling, we reran the published PnP-DM sampler on the 16 ablation images with seed 0 at each τ \tau . We saved its prior-step outputs at zero-based outer iterations 0, 25, 50, 74, and 99 of 100 and evaluated all three likelihoods at these same candidates against the quadrature reference. Relative to the original final reconstructions, the reruns change the measured score error by at most 0.0121 percentage points and the energy error by at most 6.82 × 10 − 5 6.82\times 10^{-5} nats per measurement. Table 7 reports the relative score error; UAL also has the lowest mean energy error at every sampling state and uncertainty level. At the first saved state, UAL’s mean relative image-score error ranges from 17.5% to 19.9% across uncertainty levels. sections.text: At ( s ¯ , τ ) = ( 3 , 0.5 ) (\bar{s},\tau)=(3,0.5) , UAL increases per-trajectory PSNR for all four Gaussian-deblurring samplers (Table 1 ). With the true kernel, the published DiffPIR sampler gives 30.90 dB mean per-trajectory PSNR; UAL closes 16.0% of its Published-to-Oracle PSNR gap (Table 8 ). sections.heading: D.4 Covariance-structure control and secondary metrics
sections.text: For Gaussian deblurring with PnP-DM at ( s ¯ , τ ) = ( 3 , 0.5 ) (\bar{s},\tau)=(3,0.5) , structured UAL improves reconstruction over an isotropic likelihood with the same whitened covariance trace. The isotropic covariance is S iso ​ ( x ) = [ 1 + c ⁡ ( x ) ] ​ Σ e , c ⁡ ( x ) = 1 m ​ tr ⁡ ( Σ e − 1 ​ J ψ ​ ( x ) ​ Σ ψ ​ J ψ ​ ( x ) 𝖳 ) , S_{\rm iso}(x)=[1+c(x)]\Sigma_{e},\qquad c(x)=\frac{1}{m}\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Sigma_{e}^{-1}J_{\psi}(x)\Sigma_{\psi}J_{\psi}(x)^{\mathsf{T}}\bigr), (77) where m m is the measurement dimension. Here c ⁡ ( x ) c(x) is the average added variance after noise whitening, so 1 + c ⁡ ( x ) = v ⋆ ​ ( x ) 1+c(x)=v_{\star}(x) . Both likelihoods include Gaussian normalization and differentiate their signal-dependent covariance. Structured UAL gains 0.455 ± 0.197 0.455\pm 0.197 dB over the isotropic control in per-trajectory PSNR and reduces CRPS by 0.00260 ± 0.00056 0.00260\pm 0.00056 (mean ± \pm standard error). The isotropic control produces little change from the published sampler (Table 13 ). Structured UAL improves per-trajectory PSNR over isotropic inflation on 13 of 16 Gaussian-deblurring images. In motion deblurring, isotropic inflation improves mean per-trajectory PSNR by 6.212 ± 0.398 6.212\pm 0.398 dB over the published sampler. Structured UAL adds 2.557 ± 0.317 2.557\pm 0.317 dB in per-trajectory PSNR and reduces CRPS by 0.02706 ± 0.00336 0.02706\pm 0.00336 relative to the isotropic control. The corresponding ensemble-mean PSNR margin is 4.431 ± 0.325 4.431\pm 0.325 dB. Structured UAL improves per-trajectory PSNR over isotropic inflation on 15 of 16 motion-deblurring images. These results support using the nuisance-induced covariance directions to weight the residual. In Gaussian deblurring with PnP-DM, recomputing covariance preserves the reconstruction gain when its derivatives are stopped. The stopped-derivative control removes both covariance terms in ( 6 ), so it tests their combined effect. Mean per-trajectory PSNR is 26.944 dB for the published sampler, 27.506 dB with covariance derivatives stopped, and 27.475 dB with UAL. Fixing covariance at the published sampler’s ensemble mean gives 26.964 dB, with UAL higher by 0.512 ± 0.113 0.512\pm 0.113 dB; uncertainties are standard errors across the 16 images. With fixed covariance, ensemble-mean PSNR is 29.088 dB and CRPS is 0.03484, compared with 29.388 dB and 0.03253 for the published sampler. Refreshing covariance with its derivatives stopped gives 30.304 dB and 0.02976, close to 30.259 dB and 0.02981 for UAL. We also select a fixed noise-variance multiplier by mean per-trajectory PSNR. For the scalar noise-variance multipliers v = 1 , 1.5 , 2 , 3 , 5 v=1,1.5,2,3,5 , mean per-trajectory PSNR is 26.944, 26.991, 27.007, 27.029, and 26.995 dB, respectively. UAL exceeds the selected scalar control by 0.446 ± 0.123 0.446\pm 0.123 dB, with higher PSNR on 15 of 16 images; the uncertainty is one standard error of the paired image differences. In motion deblurring, the best tested multiplier, v = 48 v=48 , gives 23.369 dB mean per-trajectory PSNR and CRPS 0.05773, compared with 26.641 dB and 0.03149 for UAL (Table 12 ). UAL gives higher mean per-trajectory PSNR on 15 of 16 images. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.29102v1 [cs.CV] 21 Oct 2026 Diffusion Posterior Sampling with Uncertain Forward Models Wentao Shangguan & Vivek K Goyal Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering Affiliation: Boston University Affiliation: Boston, MA 02215, USA Affiliation: wentaos@bu.edu, v.goyal@ieee.org Abstract Diffusion posterior samplers reconstruct signals by combining a pretrained diffusion prior with a measurement likelihood specified by a forward model and a noise model. Calibration and reference data can characterize uncertainty in the forward model’s parameters, such as blur kernels or detector responses. Fixing these parameters at estimated values leaves their uncertainty out of the likelihood, and parameter errors are thus absorbed into the reconstruction. We introduce an uncertainty-aware likelihood (UAL), a Gaussian approximation to the marginal likelihood obtained by integrating over the uncertain parameters. For each candidate signal, UAL propagates parameter uncertainty into a structured measurement covariance, reducing the quadratic penalty along residual directions that parameter variation can explain. Existing samplers can use UAL in their data updates while retaining their pretrained diffusion priors and sampling schedules. Under a fixed Gaussian nuisance model, we bound likelihood error from linearization and average divergence between the exact marginal and UAL posteriors. We compare samplers with and without UAL across six inverse problems spanning Gaussian and motion deblurring, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and fluorescence microscopy, and find improvements in reconstruction and ensemble prediction. UAL reduces geometric mean MSE by 9% to 20% across samplers in the main Gaussian-deblurring setting and by 51% to 92% in motion deblurring when non-blind samplers use the population-mean kernel. In motion deblurring, DAPS and PnP-DM with UAL also give 6.2 to 6.4 dB higher ensemble-mean PSNR than published BlindDPS and Fast Diffusion EM. On the ablation set, UAL outperforms trace-matched isotropic inflation for PnP-DM in both deblurring tasks; in motion deblurring, it also exceeds the best-tested fixed scalar data weighting by 3.3 dB for PnP-DM and 4.2 dB for DAPS in average PSNR. Figure 1: Reconstruction examples and quantitative effects of UAL across six inverse problems. Reconstruction rows show selected individual trajectories; bars summarize each evaluation set on task-specific scales. Ultrasound reports CNR and gCNR computed within each reconstruction on the contrast phantom, with one SE across its 12 paired trajectories; the delay-and-sum reference (DAS75) is shown. Other tasks report PSNR and CRPS with paired-bootstrap whiskers. 1 Introduction Diffusion posterior samplers reconstruct signals by combining a pretrained diffusion prior ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) with a measurement likelihood specified by a forward model and an observation noise model ( Chung et al., 2023b ; Wu et al., 2024 ) . Parameters in the forward model, such as a blur kernel or detector response, can remain uncertain after calibration. We treat these quantities as nuisance parameters: they affect the measurements but estimating them is not an explicit goal. Calibration and reference data provide nuisance parameter estimates and can also describe their uncertainty. Fixing these quantities at one estimate, however, leaves that uncertainty out of the reconstruction likelihood. A reconstruction process can then distort the signal to fit components of residuals caused by nuisance parameter error. In motion deblurring, for example, a kernel bank describes variation in blur direction and extent across exposures. For a candidate image and a fixed kernel, the residual between the observed and predicted measurements combines image error, kernel error, and observation noise. A point likelihood, evaluated at one fixed kernel, penalizes this residual using only the observation noise model. For each candidate image, however, the kernel statistics and forward model predict correlated measurement changes caused by kernel variation. Residuals along these predicted directions provide weaker evidence of image error than residuals with the same observation-noise penalty that kernel variation cannot explain, so they should receive smaller quadratic penalties. The same effect arises in CT, where uncertainty in the flat and dark reference fields used for calibration changes the corrected projections even for fixed acquired data ( Shi et al., 2026 ) . Non-blind diffusion posterior samplers condition on a fixed measurement model ( Chung et al., 2023b ; Kawar et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , whereas blind methods sample or estimate the nuisance parameters together with the signal ( Chung et al., 2023a ; Murata et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Some blind samplers, such as BlindDPS, train an additional diffusion prior for the nuisance parameters ( Chung et al., 2023a ) . We instead marginalize forward-model parameters using an uncertainty model specified by calibration and reference information. Let x x denote the unknown signal, y y the measurements, ψ \psi the nuisance parameters, and q q a fixed uncertainty distribution for ψ \psi . The marginal likelihood is p marg ​ ( y ∣ x ) = 𝔼 ψ ∼ q ​ [ p ⁡ ( y ∣ x , ψ ) ] . p_{\mathrm{marg}}(y\mid x)=\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim q}\!\left[p(y\mid x,\psi)\right]. We introduce an uncertainty-aware likelihood (UAL), a Gaussian approximation to the nuisance-marginal likelihood that allows this direction-dependent weighting to be incorporated into existing diffusion posterior samplers. At a candidate signal, UAL linearizes the forward model in the nuisance parameters and uses their mean and covariance to construct the measurement likelihood. UAL is exact for affine nuisance dependence with Gaussian nuisance parameters and independent Gaussian observation noise; for non-Gaussian q q , UAL uses a Gaussian with the mean and covariance of the linearized measurement model (Section 3.1 ). For a fixed Gaussian nuisance model, we bound likelihood error from linearization and the resulting posterior divergence averaged over measurements from the model (Corollary 1 ). In a fixed-sensitivity linear model with known signal covariance and matched nuisance moments, the linear estimator using UAL minimizes mean squared reconstruction error among linear estimators, averaged over signals, nuisance parameters, and observation noise. At a fixed nuisance realization, the point-likelihood estimator can instead have lower error. For a single nuisance parameter and distinct estimators, we give the crossover distance from the nuisance mean in closed form (Appendix B ). UAL incorporates calibration and reference statistics into existing samplers’ data updates while retaining their pretrained priors and sampling schedules. We evaluate it with non-blind and blind diffusion samplers on synthetic and acquired measurements: Gaussian and motion deblurring, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and fluorescence microscopy. A simpler alternative inflates the observation-noise variance, which in effect weakens the data term. For PnP-DM, the best tested scalar inflation gives mean per-trajectory PSNR of 27.03 dB in Gaussian deblurring and 23.37 dB in motion deblurring. UAL adds variance only along directions that parameter variation can explain and gives 27.48 and 26.64 dB, respectively (Section 4.3 ). UAL also improves ensemble prediction: it lowers the mean CRPS, energy, and local variogram scores for every sampler and application in Table 1 . In Gaussian deblurring, UAL more closely matches the numerically marginalized likelihood and image score than the point and isotropic alternatives; covariance controls show the reconstruction benefit of structured, candidate-dependent weighting (Section 4.3 ). Applying UAL requires nuisance means and covariances and a forward model for propagating their variation; no additional diffusion-model training is needed. Covariance factorization reduces evaluation to forming and solving a system in nuisance coordinates. In the configurations of Table 22 , UAL takes at most three times the published sampler’s wall time per trajectory, except DAPS in motion deblurring at 7.1 times (Appendix D.8 ). 2 Background and Related Work Diffusion priors for inverse problems. For fixed nuisance parameters ψ \psi and a signal prior p 0 ​ ( x ) p_{0}(x) that does not depend on ψ \psi , Bayes’ rule gives p ⁡ ( x ∣ y , ψ ) ∝ p ⁡ ( y ∣ x , ψ ) ​ p 0 ​ ( x ) p(x\mid y,\psi)\propto p(y\mid x,\psi)p_{0}(x) , where p ⁡ ( y ∣ x , ψ ) p(y\mid x,\psi) is the measurement likelihood. A pretrained diffusion model provides the prior through its denoisers or scores ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . The likelihood enters diffusion reconstruction through three common data-update forms: gradient guidance, data-fidelity optimization, and sampling-based updates. The likelihood at a noisy diffusion state x t x_{t} , p ⁡ ( y ∣ x t , ψ ) p(y\mid x_{t},\psi) , averages over possible clean signals and is generally intractable. DPS-style gradient guidance approximates it using a denoised estimate x ^ 0 ​ ( x t ) \hat{x}_{0}(x_{t}) and differentiates through that estimate ( Chung et al., 2023b ) . Π \Pi GDM propagates Gaussian approximations of clean-signal uncertainty through a fixed measurement operator to approximate the noisy-state likelihood ( Song et al., 2023 ) . Data-fidelity optimization solves a subproblem between denoising steps ( Zhu et al., 2023 ) . Sampling-based updates use the measurement in spectral coordinates ( Kawar et al., 2022 ) , in a split Gibbs sampler ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , or in annealed conditionals ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Diffusion priors with fixed-operator measurement models are also used in MRI ( Aali et al., 2025 ) , ultrasound ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , and CT ( Shi et al., 2026 ) . In these fixed-operator formulations, the likelihood conditions on a single nuisance-parameter value. For plug-and-play unadjusted Langevin sampling, Renaud et al. (2024) bound posterior error under mismatched measurement models and denoisers. UAL instead accounts for uncertainty in the forward-model parameters and enters each sampler through its existing data update (Section 3.2 ). Blind inverse problems. Blind reconstruction treats the nuisance parameters as additional inference variables. Joint samplers place a prior on them and sample them with the signal: BlindDPS couples an image diffusion model and an operator diffusion model through a shared measurement likelihood ( Chung et al., 2023a ) ; GibbsDDRM alternates approximate posterior updates under a generic operator prior ( Murata et al., 2023 ) ; and PRISM pairs a measurement-conditioned kernel prior with an unconditional image prior in a split Gibbs sampler ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . Estimation methods fit them instead: Fast Diffusion EM updates the operator in a maximization step from image samples, with denoiser-based kernel regularization ( Laroche et al., 2024 ) ; and DMPlug optimizes the input to a pretrained diffusion generator jointly with the operator parameters ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . Kernel Diffusion samples a conditional kernel distribution and uses a non-blind method to reconstruct the image ( Sanghvi et al., 2025 ) . Under the same joint model, exact joint inference and exact marginalization give the same signal posterior; the methods differ in how nuisance uncertainty reaches the signal update. UAL approximates the marginal measurement likelihood from a specified uncertainty model, without training an additional diffusion model for the nuisance parameters. Appendix C gives the image and operator updates for the evaluated samplers. Calibration and reference information. We use calibration data and reference samples to specify the means and covariances of uncertain forward-model parameters. Repeated CT flat and dark frames characterize variation in calibration fields ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , and principal-component representations of flat fields support dynamic projection normalization ( Nieuwenhove et al., 2015 ) . A motion-kernel bank describes variation in blur across exposures. ESPIRiT derives coil sensitivity maps from calibration data and permits multiple maps when a single-map model is insufficient ( Uecker et al., 2014 ) . Differences between the sound speeds provided with CUBDL acquisitions and their optimized values set the uncertainty scale for our PICMUS phantom reconstructions ( Hyun et al., 2021 ; Liebgott et al., 2016 ) . We represent the parameter variation by a distribution q q and use its mean and covariance to construct UAL (Section 3.1 ). Marginalization and UAL. Errors-in-variables models account for measurement error in the model’s input variables ( Fuller, 1987 ) . Wiesel et al. (2008) derive maximum-likelihood estimators for linear regression with Gaussian uncertainty in the model matrix, and Beck and Eldar (2010) extend them to structured perturbations. Kumar et al. (2013) linearize sampling-location errors to obtain a Gaussian likelihood with signal-dependent variance, then update the variance weights in an iterative linear estimator. Using Bayesian approximation-error modeling ( Kaipio and Somersalo, 2007 ; Kaipio and Kolehmainen, 2013 ; Nissinen et al., 2007 ) , Mozumder et al. (2016) approximately marginalize uncertain optical coefficients with an enhanced Gaussian error model whose moments are estimated from prior samples and held fixed during reconstruction. For partially known random blurs, covariance weighting gives the classical LMMSE restoration filter ( Galatsanos et al., 2000 ) . UAL adapts this Gaussian treatment of forward-model uncertainty to diffusion posterior sampling through existing samplers’ data updates, and we test it against numerical marginalization and scalar variance inflation. 3 Method 3.1 Forward model and UAL construction Let x ∈ ℝ n x\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denote the unknown signal (an image in our applications), y ∈ ℝ m y\in\mathbb{R}^{m} the measurement, and ψ ∈ ℝ P \psi\in\mathbb{R}^{P} the nuisance parameters. Additional controls examine covariance structure, recomputation and differentiation, uncertainty level, and retained rank. Published denotes the released sampler and UAL its uncertainty-aware version; each pair uses the same measurement data, diffusion checkpoint, sampling schedule, step sizes, and reconstruction seeds. Deblurring, CT, MRI, and microscopy use 50 cases, and ultrasound uses the acquired PICMUS contrast and resolution phantoms provided with DRUS; each case has 12 reconstruction seeds. The fixed deblurring ablation set contains 16 images, with 12 paired reconstruction seeds per image. Appendix C gives forward models, nuisance models, and sampler updates. We report PSNR and SSIM both as the mean over trajectories and for the ensemble-mean reconstruction. Motion deblurring is similarly insensitive to 20% changes in covariance scale (Table 17 ). 5 Conclusion and limitations UAL uses forward-model uncertainty to weight measurement-residual directions according to how well parameter variation can explain them. It enters existing samplers through their data updates without additional diffusion-model training, and it improves reconstruction in CT, MRI, and fluorescence microscopy and contrast in ultrasound. In controlled Gaussian and motion deblurring comparisons with PnP-DM, retaining covariance structure improves reconstruction beyond trace-matched isotropic inflation. Accounting for forward-model uncertainty improves ensemble prediction: UAL lowers the mean CRPS, energy, and local variogram scores in all 12 comparisons in Table 1 . For PnP-DM in Gaussian deblurring, UAL has lower mean relative image-score error than the published and isotropic likelihoods at the final reconstructions and every evaluated sampling state, using numerical marginalization as the reference. UAL’s accuracy and reconstruction benefit depend on the nuisance model and, for nonlinear nuisance dependence, on the local forward-model approximation. UAL adds computation that grows with the covariance rank and depends on the sampler (Appendix D.8 ). In deblurring, UAL keeps its gain under tested mean or covariance-scale errors of up to about 20% (Figure 12 , Table 17 ); a different motion-kernel population was not tested. References Aali et al.
